newsitem.title: FRANCE: Berisha to appeal for police, aid, from EU.
newsitem.headline: Berisha to appeal for police, aid, from EU.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said he would ask a visiting European Union delegation on Monday to send police and economic aid to help restore order to his battered country.
Berisha also said, in an interview with Europe 1 radio, that he would resign if his party lost elections in June and asserted that the widely-feared secret police had been virtually disbanded.
"Our efforts should be strongly helped by Europe," Berisha said. An EU delegation, headed by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, is due in Albania on Monday.

"We will request a major assistance to rebuild our institutions, also a very quick humanitarian assistance...and economic aid," he said of the mission. He said that Albania needed food in coming days.
EU foreign ministers decided at the weekend to send the delegation but ruled out Albania's request for military intervention to control the unrest. Many foreigners have been evacuated in the chaos.
Asked whether he would request foreign troops or police, Berisha said: "rather police to start with, because they will work with our police. It's urgent because elections have been fixed for June".
Berisha, who has resisted pressure to resign, said he would stay in power if his Democratic Party won the elections.
If the party loses, "I will immediately resign, because the president is directly elected by the parliament," he said. Berisha speaks fluent French, having once worked in Paris as a doctor.
He also said the Albanian secret police had all but been dissolved. The head of the secret police Bashkim Gazidede resigned last week, meeting one of the main demands of anti-government rebels.

"The secret police is almost entirely suppressed," he said. At another point in the interview, he went further: "The Albanian secret police no longer exists. It disbanded on its own. Most of its institutions no longer exist."
He blamed much of the violence, in which more than 100 people have died, on "bands made up of the former secret police, traffickers."
Berisha also denied that he had ever given orders for troops to fire on Albanian citizens. "There have been killed and wounded. But no one, no one, has orders to fire on the crowd," he said.
He said that, after a string of towns were seized by rebels last week, "these last days there has been a very fragile calm. The danger of a civil war has receded but the situation remains critical."
Berisha reiterated that his government had a responsibility for the crisis, triggered by the collapse of pyramid schemes in which many Albanians invested their savings.

But while he said that the government should have acted sooner to crack down on the savings projects, he added "I am firm in my belief that the main responsibility lies with those who put their money in these schemes."
